cooling with rear door heat exchanger (RDHx) for high-compute data centers

Abstract 
This study evaluates the thermal performance and energy 
efficiency of the rear door heat exchanger (RDHx) 
system, a rack-based cooling solution for high-density IT 
equipment. 
Computational 
fluid 
dynamics (CFD) 
analysis of a 150 kW IT module confirms that RDHx 
maintains ASHRAE-compliant conditions at a 24°C 
supply 
air 
temperature. 
The 
secondary 
coolant 
distribution unit (CDU) and primary chiller’s chilled 
water temperatures can be increased to 14°C and 12°C, 
respectively. A 30 MW data center model demonstrates 
improved energy chat efficiency, with cooling power 
usage effectiveness (PUE) ranging from 1.24 to 1.32. 
These findings support RDHx adoption, with future 
validation planned through a 150 kW mock-up test.

Practical Implications 
RDHx enables stable IT operations while reducing 
cooling energy consumption. Higher chilled water 
temperatures improve chiller efficiency and lower 
operational costs. The quantified energy distribution 
guides optimized data center cooling strategies. 
Introduction 
Data centers are at the core of digital transformation, 
driving advancements in artificial intelligence, big data, 
and cloud computing, which are reshaping various 
industries through digital integration (Cho et al., 2022). 
As IT infrastructure evolves, increasing power demands 
necessitate efficient cooling solutions while maintaining 
energy efficiency and thermal stability. Historically, 
server racks operated at 2-5 kW per rack, but power 
density has steadily increased, reaching a global average 
of 8.4 kW by 2020 (AFCOM, 2021). High-performance 
computing (HPC) applications have further intensified 
this trend, with some racks now exceeding 50 kW. To 
manage the resulting thermal challenges, cooling 
strategies have been categorized into room-based, row-
based, and rack-based approaches (Cho and Lim, 2023). 
However, traditional air cooling methods are nearing 
their practical limits, prompting a shift toward liquid 
cooling, which offers significantly higher cooling 
capacity (Khalaj and Halgamuge, 2017). Among liquid 
cooling methods, rack-based cooling with RDHx has 
emerged as a promising solution for high-density IT 
environments. Recent research has explored data-driven 
and state-space modeling approaches for temperature 
prediction, improving accuracy and computational 
efficiency (Tong et al., 2023). Additionally, rack-
mounted cooling units and multi-stage liquid cooling 
configurations have been developed to enhance thermal 
performance (Li et al., 2023). Hybrid cooling systems 
integrating heat pipes and vapor compression technology 
have also demonstrated potential for improving power 
usage effectiveness (Sun et al., 2023). While these 
studies have advanced cooling efficiency and predictive 
modeling, a comprehensive quantitative analysis of 
RDHx energy and thermal performance remains limited. 
This study aims to provide an in-depth numerical 
analysis of RDHx cooling for high-density IT 
environments. By evaluating its thermal behavior, 
energy efficiency, and overall impact on data center 
operations, this research offers critical insights for 
optimizing RDHx implementation in next-generation 
data centers. 
Numerical Methods 
Data center cooling is broadly classified into air cooling 
and liquid cooling (Li et al., 2024). While air cooling 
remains the most widely used method, accounting for 
over 99% of operational data centers (Heydari, 2021), its 
power density limit of 30 kW per rack necessitates a 
transition to liquid cooling (ASHRAE TC 9.9, 2019). 
However, liquid-cooled IT equipment is not yet widely 
adopted due to compatibility, infrastructure requirements, 
and operational risks (Zhan et al., 2020). The RDHx is a 
hybrid cooling solution, combining air cooling for IT 
equipment with liquid cooling at the rack level, offering 
improved thermal performance and energy efficiency 
(Jiang et al., 2021). 
In this study, an RDHx-based 150 kW IT module was 
designed and analyzed. The module comprises 10 rack 
servers (15 kW per rack) with RDHx units installed at 
the rear for cooling (Figure 1). Unlike conventional 
cooling methods, RDHx eliminates the hot aisle, 
containing airflow entirely within the cold aisle to 
prevent air bypass and recirculation. This configuration 
allows an increase in supply air temperature (SAT) to 
24°C, enabling higher coolant temperatures of 14°C at 
the CDU level and 12°C at the primary chiller system, 
significantly improving energy efficiency.

exchanging heat with the primary chilled water loop. 
Thermal Performance 
The inlet air temperature of IT equipment is a key 
parameter in data center thermal management (ASHRAE, 
2021). According to ASHRAE TC 9.9, Class A1 data 
centers should maintain an acceptable inlet air 
temperature range of 15-32°C, with a recommended 
range of 18-27°C. For high-density applications (Class 
H1), the recommended range is 18-22°C, with an 
allowable range of 5-25°C (Herrlin and Sharp, 2005). 
The RDHx system in this study operates within these 
guidelines while optimizing cooling efficiency.

A CFD simulation was performed using 6SigmaDCX, a 
specialized software for data center airflow modeling. 
The simulation evaluated airflow distribution and 
temperature stability within the 150 kW IT module 
(Figure 2). The boundary conditions for the CFD 
analysis, including airflow rates and thermal loads, are 
presented in Table 2. The computational model consists 
of a 12.0 m × 15.6 m × 5.0 m module containing 10 rack 
servers, 10 RDHx units, and an enclosed cold aisle. The 
total number of grids used in the CFD simulation was 
539,286. A mesh independence study confirmed that 
increasing the grid resolution beyond 540,000 cells did 
not significantly impact simulation accuracy.

A 30 MW reference data center was modeled to evaluate 
cooling energy performance. The facility, located in 
Seoul, Korea, is designed for a total IT load of 30 MW, 
with 2,000 rack servers (15 kW per rack) utilizing

(6 MW per floor), operating under a centralized cooling 
system (Figure 3 and Table 3). The central cooling 
system consists of six 6,000 kW chillers (1,800 RT each), 
maintaining a chilled water supply temperature of 12°C 
and condenser water return temperature of 32°C. The 
cooling system is configured with N+1 redundancy, 
ensuring operational reliability.

Numerical Results 
The results of this study are divided into two main 
aspects: thermal performance evaluation and cooling 
energy efficiency assessment. Through CFD simulations 
and energy modeling, the effectiveness of the RDHx 
system in high-density IT environments is analyzed to 
validate its thermal stability and energy efficiency.

Thermal Performance 
The thermal performance of the RDHx system was 
assessed using CFD analysis, confirming that when the 
SAT is set to 24°C, the inlet air temperature of IT 
equipment remains within the ASHRAE-recommended 
range (ASHRAE, 2021). The RDHx system effectively 
minimizes air distribution losses by significantly 
shortening airflow pathways, ensuring stable airflow and 
uniform temperature distribution. 
The analysis of air temperature distribution (Figure 5) 
indicates that the hot air discharged from IT equipment 
is effectively cooled as it passes through the RDHx unit 
installed at the rear of each rack.  
Figure 6 presents the mean inlet air temperature of rack 
servers in the RDHx cooling system when the SAT is set 
to 24°C. The results indicate that the average inlet 
temperature across all racks remains within a narrow 
range of 24.12°C to 24.29°C, demonstrating a uniform 
cooling 
performance. 
The 
maximum 
temperature 
deviation among the racks is 0.17°C, confirming 
minimal thermal variation and effective air distribution. 
These findings highlight the stability and consistency of 
the RDHx system in maintaining optimal IT operating 
conditions.

The airflow velocity distribution analysis (Figure 7) 
shows that the velocity of exhaust air from IT servers 
exceeds 5 m/s, whereas the air discharged from the 
RDHx unit is 2-3 m/s, indicating effective heat exchange. 
Unlike traditional room-based or row-based cooling 
methods, RDHx cooling maintains uniform airflow at 
approximately 2 m/s across all racks, preventing 
hotspots and ensuring stable cooling efficiency. 
Energy Efficiency 
The impact of RDHx on energy efficiency was evaluated 
based on its cooling energy consumption and PUE. The 
thermal performance results indicate that raising the 
SAT to 24°C allows for an increase in chilled water 
temperatures at both the CDU and chiller levels, leading 
to improved overall cooling efficiency. 
An analysis of the annual IT load and cooling demand 
reveals that the total IT load of 30 MW remains stable 
throughout the year, resulting in a consistent cooling 
requirement (Figure 8). The RDHx units remove 
approximately 32,333-33,000 kW of heat per hour, 
adjusting the SAT dynamically to maintain a 10°C 
temperature differential (ΔT) between supply and return 
air temperatures. The energy consumption of RDHx fans 
is estimated at 1,335 kW per hour, translating to an 
annual energy consumption of 11,577 MWh.

Further analysis of chiller and pump energy consumption 
indicates that the five chillers supplying chilled water at 
12°C operate continuously throughout the year, 
consuming 32,534 MWh annually. The cooling tower 
fans operate at a constant rate, contributing 3,252 MWh 
to annual energy consumption. Additionally, water 
circulation pumps, including chilled water pumps, 
condenser water pumps, and coolant pumps, account for 
a combined annual consumption of 23,674 MWh. 
Table 5 summarizes the overall PUEcooling and energy 
distribution, revealing that the total IT energy 
consumption amounts to 260,147 MWh, while the 
cooling infrastructure accounts for 71,037 MWh, 
resulting in a PUEcooling of 1.273. This indicates that 27.3% 
of total data center energy consumption is attributed to 
cooling operations, which is significantly lower than 
conventional room-based air-cooling systems, which 
typically report PUE values above 1.4 (AFCOM, 2021). 
The breakdown of cooling energy consumption shows 
that 46% is consumed by chillers, 21% by RDHx fan 
power, and 33% by pumps, highlighting the major 
contributors to the overall cooling load (Figure 9).

Seasonal variations in cooling efficiency were also 
examined (Figure 10), showing that the PUEcooling 
fluctuates between 1.25 and 1.33, with an average of 
1.27. These fluctuations are primarily influenced by 
changes in the condenser water return temperature 
(RCWT) during winter, highlighting the importance of 
seasonal cooling tower adjustments in optimizing chiller 
COP and reducing overall energy consumption (Figure 
11). 
Discussion 
The results of this study demonstrate that rack-based 
cooling with RDHx provides significant thermal stability 
and energy efficiency improvements in high-density IT 
environments. The discussion focuses on the comparison 
with conventional cooling methods, implications for 
energy efficiency, and potential optimizations for future 
data centers. 
RDHx, as a rack-based cooling solution, effectively 
minimizes air distribution losses compared to room-
based and row-based cooling. Traditional air-cooled data 
centers rely on computer room air conditioning (CRAC) 
or computer room air handling (CRAH) units, which 
require longer air pathways and are susceptible to hot air 
recirculation and bypass issues. The CFD analysis 
confirms that RDHx eliminates the formation of a hot 
aisle, ensuring that cooled air is directly supplied to IT 
equipment, leading to lower temperature variations 
among racks. 
Additionally, while air-cooled data centers typically 
struggle to maintain stable temperatures above 20 kW 
per rack, RDHx efficiently manages loads exceeding 30 
kW per rack. The mean inlet air temperature across all 
racks remained within a narrow range of 24.12°C to 
24.29°C, highlighting its ability to provide consistent 
cooling even under high-power density conditions. 
Although RDHx offers considerable improvements, 
further optimizations can enhance its performance and 
adaptability for next-generation data centers. One critical 
area for improvement is the integration of hybrid cooling 
systems, which combine RDHx with direct liquid 
cooling (DLC) for heterogeneous IT loads.

on real-time workload variations.

efficiency of rack-based cooling with RDHx in high-
density data centers, demonstrating its effectiveness as a 
sustainable and efficient cooling solution. The findings 
confirm that RDHx minimizes air distribution losses, 
maintains

Abstract: This study evaluates the thermal performance and energy efficiency of the rear door heat exchanger (RDHx) system, a rack-based cooling solution for high-density IT equipment. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) analysis of a 150 kW IT module confirms that RDHx maintains ASHRAE-compliant conditions at a 24°C supply air temperature. The secondary coolant distribution unit (CDU) and primary chiller’s chilled water temperatures can be increased to 14°C and 12°C, respectively. A 30 MW data center model demonstrates improved energy chat efficiency, with cooling power usage effectiveness (PUE) ranging from 1.24 to 1.32. These findings support RDHx adoption, with future validation planned through a 150 kW mock-up test.
